title: Street Fighter II: The World Warrior
japaneseTitle: ストリートファイターII
shortDescription: Capcom's definitive competitive arcade fighter introducing command motion inputs, six-button controls, and the accidental discovery of the combo system.
historicalSignificance: Created the modern fighting game genre, sparked the 1990s worldwide arcade renaissance, established competitive esports tournament culture, and redefined 1-on-1 multiplayer interaction.

editorialContent.overview: Directed by Akira Nishitani and designed by Akira Yasuda (Akiman) with music composed by Yoko Shimomura and Isao Abe, Street Fighter II: The World Warrior premiered on Capcom's CP System (CPS-1) arcade hardware in February 1991. The game revolutionized interactive competition by pivoting away from cooperative side-scrolling beat-'em-ups toward high-intensity, head-to-head personal duels, sparking a global coin-op boom that revitalized amusement arcades for a decade.
editorialContent.gameplayMechanics: Featuring eight distinct international martial artists—each with unique bounding hitboxes, recovery frames, and movement rates—Street Fighter II formalized directional joystick motion commands (Quarter-Circle Forward 'Hadoken', Z-motion 'Shoryuken', and charge buffering 'Sonic Boom'). An accidental programming phenomenon, where hitstun animations permitted an unblockable follow-up attack before the defender recovered, birthed the 'combo system' that remains the universal mechanical foundation of competitive fighting games.
editorialContent.technicalInnovation: Built for Capcom's Motorola 68000-based CPS-1 board running at 10 MHz with a secondary Zilog Z80 managing sound, Street Fighter II displayed 384 × 224 resolution graphics with 4,096 simultaneous on-screen colors and multi-layered parallax scrolling backdrops. The cabinet introduced a standardized six-button control array consisting of Light, Medium, and Heavy Punches and Kicks.
editorialContent.culturalImpact: Street Fighter II generated billions of dollars in arcade revenue and became a defining cultural touchstone of the 1990s. The 1992 home conversion for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System sold over six million copies, solidifying Nintendo's 16-bit console dominance. The culture of gathered arcade onlookers, coin-on-the-glass queue etiquette, and regional mastery laid the direct historical groundwork for the modern global fighting game community (FGC) and competitive esports tournaments such as Evolution (EVO).
editorialContent.preservationNotes: Preserved across original CPS-1 ROM revisions (World, Japan, USA sets with minor damage/dizzy balance variances). Emulation preservation requires reproducing the exact CPS-1 raster interrupt line timing and Yamaha YM2151 FM / OKI MSM6295 ADPCM voice playback.
